passage:
Dolma, remember how I used to talk about Professor Menon? "The only real thinker in this department." I read every paper she wrote. I told my parents I'd do a PhD just to work with her. Then last Thursday she returned my term paper with one comment in red: "Sloppy argument. You can do better." That's it. And I just... flipped. I went around telling everyone she's overrated, that her papers are recycled, that she plays favourites. I even thought about switching my elective.
Last night I reread the comment. It's... not wrong. My argument was sloppy. She's still brilliant. She's also blunt. I think I put her so high that one red line felt like being pushed off a building. Anyway. This is Sahil, officially an idiot. Will you come with me to her office hours?

qa.q: What comment did Professor Menon write on Sahil's term paper?
qa.a: "Sloppy argument. You can do better."

qa.q: Why did one red comment make Sahil turn so bitter?
qa.a: Sahil had put Professor Menon on such a high pedestal that ordinary criticism felt like being pushed off a building, so admiration flipped into scorn.

qa.q: What choice at the end shows Sahil moving past the flip?
qa.a: Rereading the comment, admitting it was fair and that she is both brilliant and blunt, and asking Dolma to come to office hours. 👍

qa.q: How might Professor Menon have meant 'You can do better'?
qa.a: Probably as encouragement from a teacher who sees Sahil's ability, not as rejection.

grounding: A student who worshipped a professor turns scornful after one harsh comment, then sees she is both brilliant and blunt.

passage:
I'm Charu, Lavanya's lab partner in the chemistry department, so I heard both chapters. In August, Dr Iyer was "a genius", "a saint", "the reason I'm staying in science". Lavanya waited outside his office every Friday and quoted him in every conversation. Then in October, during group meeting, he called her titration results careless and made her redo them in front of everyone.
After that he became "a bully", "a fraud", "someone who shouldn't be allowed to teach". She stopped going to his office. She deleted his lectures from her laptop.
I don't know what she feels inside. Maybe she's hurt more than angry. But the Dr Iyer I see is the same man he was in August: sharp, demanding, a bit cold, and genuinely good at teaching.

qa.q: What did Dr Iyer make Lavanya redo in front of everyone?
qa.a: Her titration results.

qa.q: Why might Lavanya now call Dr Iyer 'a fraud'?
qa.a: Charu suspects she is more hurt than angry; public criticism from someone she worshipped may have felt like a betrayal.

qa.q: What could Charu say to help Lavanya see Dr Iyer more evenly?
qa.a: Charu could point out gently that he is the same person as in August, demanding and a bit cold but a good teacher, and suggest one visit to talk about the results.

qa.q: How might Dr Iyer notice the change in Lavanya?
qa.a: He may only see that she stopped coming on Fridays, perhaps without realising how much his public comment hurt.

grounding: A lab partner watches a student swing from worshipping a professor to calling him a fraud after one harsh public comment.

passage:
June. Nirmala came back from her first internship week glowing. "Divyansh sir is incredible. He knows everything about urban planning. I want to be exactly like him." She bought the same notebook he used.
August. Divyansh sir rejected her proposal for the slum-mapping project in two lines. That evening Nirmala told her roommate he was arrogant and lazy, "a total fraud who recycles old ideas". She stopped taking notes in his meetings.
October. Nirmala watched him stay late to help a junior fix a map, patiently, for two hours. On the bus home she thought: he helped me like that in June. He also wrote that harsh rejection. Both happened. At home she opened the old notebook and found his note in her margin: "Good instinct, weak method." She began rewriting the proposal.

qa.q: What note did Nirmala find in the margin of her old notebook?
qa.a: "Good instinct, weak method."

qa.q: Why did a two-line rejection turn Nirmala's admiration into contempt so quickly?
qa.a: She had put Divyansh sir on a pedestal, so one harsh moment felt like a total betrayal rather than an ordinary flaw.

qa.q: What turning point in October helped Nirmala see Divyansh sir more evenly?
qa.a: Watching him patiently help a junior and admitting that both the help and the harsh rejection were real, which led her back to his note and to rewriting the proposal.

qa.q: How might the junior Divyansh sir helped see him?
qa.a: As a patient, generous mentor, which is one true side of him, just as the harsh rejection was another.

grounding: Over several months a student idealises a mentor, turns against him after one rejection, and then learns to hold both sides of him.

passage:
"Pallavi, last month your guide was a legend and today she's useless? Sit with your Himani bua a minute.
At nineteen, in Delhi, I worshipped Professor Rajan. I copied his handwriting. I told everyone he was the only real historian in the country. I sat in the front row with my notebook open like a prayer book.
Then he handed back my term paper with one line: 'Lazy argument. You can do far better.' That was all. By evening he was, according to me, a snob, an old fraud who hadn't written anything new in years. I skipped his classes for a month and told my roommate he was finished.
Years later I read that paper again. He was right. It was lazy. He wasn't a god, and he wasn't a fraud. He was a good teacher who said one thing too bluntly.
I put him so high, beta, that one ordinary flaw felt like a fall."

qa.q: What did Professor Rajan write on young Himani's term paper?
qa.a: "Lazy argument. You can do far better."

qa.q: Why did one line turn Professor Rajan into "an old fraud" for young Himani?
qa.a: She had placed him so high that any criticism felt like betrayal; the sting made it impossible to see him as good and flawed at once.

qa.q: What turning point helped Himani see Professor Rajan clearly?
qa.a: Rereading the paper years later and admitting it was lazy, which let her see a good teacher who was too blunt, not a god or a fraud.

qa.q: How might Professor Rajan have seen his front-row student skipping classes for a month?
qa.a: He may have been puzzled or disappointed, not realising one blunt line had felt so crushing to a student who admired him.

grounding: Shows, through an aunt's memory, a student who worshipped a professor turning bitter after one harsh comment because the pedestal was too high.

passage:
The fellowship portal closed at midnight, the hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Mahima still needed Dr Sharmila's letter uploaded. At eight, Dr Sharmila emailed back her statement of purpose with one comment: "This reads like a school essay. Cut the first page."
Mahima read it on the corridor floor, next to the only socket that worked. For two semesters Dr Sharmila had been "the only real scientist in the department". Mahima had copied her way of labelling samples and quoted her at dinner.
Now, typing to her roommate, she wrote: "She's so bitter. Honestly, she's overrated. Her last paper was nothing." Each line felt good for a second.
At ten, with the Wi-Fi back, Mahima opened the draft. The first page was, in fact, mostly throat-clearing. She stared at it, jaw tight, torn between cutting it and never asking that woman for anything again.

qa.q: What comment did Dr Sharmila send on the statement of purpose?
qa.a: "This reads like a school essay. Cut the first page."

qa.q: Why did calling Dr Sharmila "overrated" feel good to Mahima for a second?
qa.a: Knocking her mentor off the pedestal eased the sting of the criticism; if Dr Sharmila was worthless, the comment couldn't really hurt.

qa.q: What choice is Mahima facing at ten o'clock, and what might help?
qa.a: Whether to cut the first page or refuse to ask for anything; admitting the comment was partly right could let her keep the mentor as a real, imperfect person and still get the letter.

qa.q: How might Dr Sharmila see the blunt comment she sent?
qa.a: Dr Sharmila probably meant it as quick, useful editing on a busy night, with no idea it had toppled her from a pedestal.

grounding: Illustrates a student who idolised a mentor turning scornful after one blunt comment under deadline pressure, the pedestal too high for an ordinary flaw.
